channel.title: Ajahn Funn Ācāro Quotes
channel.description: Dhamma quotes by Ajahn Funn Ācāro, updated every 24 hours

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Let the body be at ease. After all, you want ease. Make your mind empty. Make it still. Whatever it’s stuck on, whatever…
item.description:
Have Compassion for Yourself: Look at Your Own Heart

Let the body be at ease. After all, you want ease. Make your mind empty. Make it still. Whatever it’s stuck on, whatever it’s snared by, disentangle it right now. When you die, you can’t disentangle things. When the time comes, you can’t disentangle things. But right now you can. When the harm of your actions comes to you, you can’t stop it. So counteract it now from the start. When the time comes, you’ll go running to this or that venerable old monk to show you some compassion. Whoever’s in trouble will go running to them, to ask for compassion. The problem is that you don’t show any compassion for yourself.

So have some compassion for yourself. Look at yourself. When you’re sitting in meditation like this, you can’t get devas, Indras, or Brahmās to do your looking for you. So sit and look at yourself. Are you happy or miserable? Good or bad? Try to see for yourself. It’s not that the weather’s good or the weather’s bad. Look. When there’s suffering, it’s not that the weather’s suffering. It’s your heart. So look.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: They teach us to meditate to know a calm mind — whether the mind is good or not. When it is calm, it…
item.description:
Vipassanā: Knowing the Origin and Cessation of Saṅkhāra

They teach us to meditate to know a calm mind — whether the mind is good or not. When it is calm, it becomes clear, giving rise to vipassanā-ñāṇa (insight knowledge). What does it know? It knows the origin of saṅkhāra, knows the cessation of saṅkhāra — that is vipassanā. It knows the origin and cessation of saṅkhāra, knows the suffering and the danger in saṅkhāra. When it sees the suffering, the danger, the peril of saṅkhāra, it cuts off. It does not want suffering, does not want danger. See? Where does it come from? It knows the origin but not the cessation. Where do all these saṅkhāras come from? They come from our own mind — the concocting, the fabricating, the thinking, the intending. Where does the intending come from? Now, having heard and listened: ehipassiko — "come and see." Call all beings to come see the Dhamma. Where to see the Dhamma? See our own rūpa-dhamma (material phenomena) and nāma-dhamma (mental phenomena). Rūpa-dhamma is our own physical body. Come see: two arms, two legs, one head.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore, let us all strive to practice meditation, to focus and look, to determine and observe. You don't need to find something elsewhere…
item.description:
Observing What Is Yours: Everything Is Already Within Yourself

Therefore, let us all strive to practice meditation, to focus and look, to determine and observe. You don't need to find something elsewhere to observe. Observe what is yours. You already have everything within yourself. Emptiness is already there. Non-emptiness is already there. Happiness is already there. Suffering is already there. Everything is here right now. Observe what you have. However it is established, keep watching it just like that. Watch to know. And do not grasp this or that as a self, as a soul. The matter is simply that. We must all understand this point. That is why we come to do kammaṭṭhāna – kamma means action, what we do; ṭhāna means foundation, place. Establish it to abide. If it is empty, know it. If it is not empty, know it. To abandon, we must contemplate the basic kammaṭṭhāna. The teacher taught the basic kammaṭṭhāna so that we would know according to reality. He taught about hair so that we would know what hair is like. Is it a person? Is it something? Is this hair clean or unclean? This is the method to remove our lust, greed, hatred, and delusion, to remove our craving concerning self-identity.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore He said: suffering (dukkha) should be comprehended, should be contemplated, leading to its origin (samudaya). We all know about samudaya – beings…
item.description:
Tracing Dependent Origination Back to Ignorance (Avijjā)

Therefore He said: suffering (dukkha) should be comprehended, should be contemplated, leading to its origin (samudaya). We all know about samudaya – beings are sunk in the great ocean, as prey for fish. That is the case. Pāpo pāpaṃ – sunk in the great ocean, meaning deluded by conventions (sammuti). The Buddha investigated: where does suffering come from? He traced it back upstream. At first He contemplated: where does suffering come from? What are its causes and conditions? It comes from illness, disease, affliction. Where do those come from? They come from aging, decrepitude, deterioration. Where does that come from? From birth. Where does birth come from? From becoming (bhava) – that is, taking a state of being. Where does that becoming come from? He contemplated: it comes from clinging (upādāna). Wherever we cling, we take becoming there. Look: our becoming, small and large – becoming comes from clinging. Where does clinging come from? From craving (taṇhā). Where does craving come from? From feeling (vedanā) – painful feeling, pleasant feeling. Where do these feelings come from? From contact (phassa). Where does contact come from? From the sense bases (āyatana) – eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind. Where do these sense bases come from? From mind-and-body (nāmarūpa). Where does nāmarūpa come from? From consciousness (viññāṇa) – rebirth-linking consciousness. Where does consciousness come from? From saṅkhārā, fabrications. Where do saṅkhārā come from? From ignorance (avijjā).

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Thus you should all know na and mo. Only then can the heart be protected. Right now, we do not know na, we…
item.description:
Contemplate the 32 Parts: No Person, Just Bile, Phlegm, Pus, Blood, Urine

Thus you should all know na and mo. Only then can the heart be protected. Right now, we do not know na, we do not know mo, so we cannot protect our own heart. Why are we contemplating this? So that we will not grieve or lament. When we must inevitably part from everything we love and cherish, when we are separated, we will have sorrow, grief, lamentation, and longing for one another.

So we quickly contemplate this now, while we are still together. When the time comes for us to depart, we will not be attached or worried about anything at all. That is why we contemplate this matter of being a self, a being, a person, a "me", a "him", a woman, a man, a monk, a novice. We grasp at na and mo — that is the problem. Look and see: delusion about self, delusion about being, delusion about person, delusion about "me" and "him" — this is what gets stuck. We contemplate na, and then we will not be deluded.

What is na? Pittaṃ — bile, semhaṃ — phlegm, pubbo — pus, lohitaṃ — blood, sedo — sweat, medo — fat, assu — tears, vasā — lymph, kheḷo — saliva, siṅghāṇikā — snot, lasikā — synovial fluid, muttaṃ — urine. Where is the person in these? Aren't they all just things to be discarded? This is what we should contemplate with certainty. Do not doubt, waver, or be uncertain in your mind.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: The “heavenly messengers” are constantly warning us. If we sit for a long time, they give their warning. If we stand for a…
item.description:
The Heavenly Messengers Warn Us in Every Posture

The “heavenly messengers” are constantly warning us. If we sit for a long time, they give their warning. If we stand for a long time, walk for a long time, lie down for a long time, they give their warning. No matter what our posture, they warn us—“pain, pain, pain, pain, pain”—but we don’t listen. These are heaps of pain, but we don’t listen. When there are aches and pains from sitting long, we change our position. We keep pushing things off for later like this, but if we keep following that strategy, we’ll reach the point where it runs out. That’s the way it is. If we lie down for a long time, there’s pain again. Try lying down for a whole day or a whole night—it’s painful, no matter which way you lie down. You turn over on this side, turn over on that, but you keep running into pain everywhere. If you walk for a long time, there’s pain again. Stand for a long time, there’s pain again. Every posture is painful. That’s why the body is called a heap of suffering.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Sit comfortably. Make your body comfortable. Adopt a posture that is dignified, bright, and smiling. When the body is comfortable, then make the…
item.description:
Reciting Buddho, Buddho – Focusing the Mind on the Knower

Sit comfortably. Make your body comfortable. Adopt a posture that is dignified, bright, and smiling. When the body is comfortable, then make the mind comfortable. Draw the eyes inward to the heart. Draw the ears inward as well. When the mind is comfortable, recollect the virtues of the Buddha. Have confidence that the Buddha is in the mind, the Dhamma is in the mind, the Noble Saṅgha is in the mind. Then reflect to see whether they really are in the mind. Think "Buddho" – where does it know? It knows in our own mind. Think "Dhammo" – where is it? It's in our mind. Think "Saṅgho" – where is it? You think it in your own mind. Oh, the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha are right here, in our mind – not elsewhere. Having that confidence, then recite the meditation word: Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho three times, then condense it to one word. Think "Buddho, Buddho". Close your eyes, shut your mouth. Focus your eyes to look at the place where you are recollecting "Buddho". Where is it recollected? Let your ears listen to that recollection of "Buddho". Let your mindfulness stare at that recollection: "Buddho, Buddho". Why look? Look to know whether this self of ours is happy or suffering, whether it is good or evil – as already explained.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: These are the Sutta, the Vinaya, the Paramattha. Dhammaṃ ve rakkhati dhammacāriṃ – "Dhamma indeed protects the one who practices Dhamma." That is…
item.description:
Dhamma Protects Those Who Practice Dhamma

These are the Sutta, the Vinaya, the Paramattha. Dhammaṃ ve rakkhati dhammacāriṃ – "Dhamma indeed protects the one who practices Dhamma." That is the Three Entities. Therefore it is said that Dhamma protects the one who practices Dhamma. If any being practices Dhamma well, Dhamma brings goodness to them. If that being practices Dhamma badly, Dhamma brings badness to them. We who are sitting here are the same. What is it? We have a similar form, the same four elements, five aggregates, six sense-bases. But our forms are not identical: some are dark, some are white, some tall, some short. Why? Whoever practices well, Dhamma gives goodness to them. Whoever practices badly, Dhamma gives badness to them. It is not that parents caused us to be born blind. Parents cannot do that, doctors cannot do that. We did it ourselves. This is the practice.

Having heard this, opanayiko – bring it inside, know it for oneself. This is the practice that has been brought to remind us. May it be a basis for listening, for the pāramī of wisdom for all of you. When you have heard it, practice yoniso manasikāra (wise attention). Let us all determine and remember it in our hearts, then practice and train ourselves in the Dhamma teachings as have been expounded. May you all have happiness and prosperity. Evaṃ – thus it is.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: The Dhamma belongs to each person who gives rise to it, who does it. This is why the Buddha taught us, but people…
item.description:
The Dhamma Protects Those Who Practice the Dhamma

The Dhamma belongs to each person who gives rise to it, who does it. This is why the Buddha taught us, but people don’t believe in his teachings. Whoever comes wants to engage in lots of conversation. Provincial governors, chief justices, judges: All kinds of people come to see me. Even crazy people come. Victims of black magic come. Every kind of person comes. People without children who want children. People with lots of children who don’t want children. People who try to fashion what they want, but they’re no good at fashioning. The Dhamma fashions for us, but we’re no good at fashioning our ears, eyes, and noses—because we don’t listen to the Dhamma.

We have to practice the Dhamma. Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāriṁ: The Dhamma protects those who practice the Dhamma. Living beings depend on the Dhamma; the Dhamma depends on living beings. Those who don’t practice the Dhamma will bring lack of wellness on themselves. Those who practice will bring wellness on themselves. To bring wellness, you sit in concentration and watch, as I’ve already explained. When your heart is well, when it experiences well-being and ease, then whatever level of becoming and birth you go to, you’ll have well-being and ease. If your heart is suffering, in turmoil, hot with trouble, you’ll receive that as a result. When you’re reborn, your body will be deformed. That’s how it happens. This is what’s important, which is why you should try to know and understand.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: When our mind is good, whatever we do is good, whatever we seek is good. Know this goodness. Is it as explained? Our…
item.description:
What Suffering Is Like: Mind Not Calm, Not Good – Miserable, Troubled

When our mind is good, whatever we do is good, whatever we seek is good. Know this goodness. Is it as explained? Our mind is Buddho — joyful, bright, cool in body and cool in heart, no suffering, no heat. Buddho is joyful, Buddho is radiant, Buddho is clear. When it is clear, it sees itself, sees its own form, sees us and others. The clear mind, the pure mind, free from suffering, free from faults, free from danger, free from enmity, free from evil and depravity, free from misery and poverty. What poverty could there be? Our mind is good, our mind is not poor, our mind is not suffering — where would suffering come from? See? It is not that the sky or air suffers. See and know. We have trained because we want to know what happiness is and what suffering is. Happiness is as explained just now. What is suffering like? It is the mind not calm, the mind not good. A mind not good is miserable, troubled, agitated. This causes beings to experience suffering and hardship in the present and the future. Some people: why does their studying not go well? Why does their work not go well? Why do they lose money in business? Why do they not get the rank and status they want? Because their mind is not good.
